analysis.one_liner: Strengthens equal-pay enforcement for women and bans employers from asking salary history or silencing pay talk.
analysis.headline: The Senate labor committee approved the bill and put it on the Senate calendar in July 2023, but it never came up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would tighten the Equal Pay Act so employers must prove a pay gap between men and women comes from a real, job-related business need. It would ban employers from punishing workers for discussing wages, from requiring workers to sign away their right to talk about pay, and from asking job applicants what they earned before. It would also add compensatory and punitive damages for victims, allow pay discrimination cases to proceed as class actions, require large employers to report pay data by sex, race, and ethnicity, and create negotiation-skills training grants for women and girls.
analysis.who_benefits: Women workers, especially women of color, who are paid less than male colleagues for the same work. They would get stronger legal remedies, easier class-action lawsuits, protection against retaliation for sharing wage information, and salary-history rules that stop past low pay from following them to the next job.

how_it_helps.text: Employers could only justify a pay gap with a bona fide, job-related factor that accounts for the entire differential and is consistent with business necessity [S2][S3].
Workers could not be required to sign contracts or waivers banning wage disclosure, and retaliation for inquiring about, discussing, or disclosing wages would be unlawful [S2][S3].
Employers could not rely on or seek a job applicant's wage history, with civil penalties up to $10,000 per offense and damages to affected applicants [S3].

Victims could recover compensatory damages, and punitive damages where the employer acted with malice or reckless indifference, plus expert fees, and pay discrimination claims could be maintained as class actions [S3].

Employers with 100 or more employees would have to report compensation, hiring, termination, and promotion data disaggregated by sex, race, and ethnicity, with aggregate data published to help enforcement [S3].
The Department of Labor would run grants for negotiation-skills training for women and girls and conduct studies and public education on pay disparities [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, particularly large ones, bear new compliance costs: pay-data reporting, higher litigation exposure from expanded damages and class actions, and penalties for salary-history questions. Small businesses are exempt to the same extent they are exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act.

drawbacks.text: The bill exposes employers to unlimited compensatory and punitive damages and expanded class actions for pay claims, a cost honest supporters acknowledge as the price of stronger deterrence [S3].

Employers would bear the burden of proving any pay differential is job-related and consistent with business necessity, and employees could defeat that defense by showing a cheaper alternative practice the employer refused to adopt — a shifting of proof that business groups in prior Congresses argued would drive litigation rather than workplace change [S2][S3].
Defining workplaces in the same county as the 'same establishment' broadens which pay comparisons count as illegal discrimination, extending compliance obligations across locations [S3].

The bill's own findings concede that roughly 40 percent of the pay gap remains unexplained after controlling for education, occupation, experience, and other factors, so some pay differences employers treat as market-based would face legal challenge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers whose pay reflects discrimination rather than job-related factors, the bill offers real remedies: stronger damages, protection against pay secrecy, and a salary-history ban that stops past underpayment from compounding. The costs fall on employers, especially the compliance and litigation burden on large companies, and some disputes would inevitably target pay differences driven by legitimate factors. The small-business exemption and technical assistance provisions modestly limit that burden, but the expanded damages and class-action provisions are the price of deterrence, not an accident.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate labor committee approved it and put it on the Senate's waiting list for floor business in July 2023, but no senator ever got the chance to vote on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the bill on March 9, 2023, and it was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S1][S5].
All 48 Senate Democrats and 3 of 4 independents cosponsored it — 51 cosponsors in total, with no Republicans [S4].
The committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment on June 21, 2023, and Senator Sanders formally reported it on July 18, 2023 [S5].
The same day, the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, meaning it was waiting for the chamber's leadership to schedule floor time [S5].
No further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that would have faced stronger equal-pay enforcement, new pay-data reporting requirements, and expanded damages exposure are better off because the bill never got a vote. Workers who might have used its remedies to close pay gaps are worse off.

sides.party_line_note: Every Senate Democrat and three independents cosponsored; not a single Republican did, so with the Senate's 60-vote threshold for moving most bills the bill had no realistic path without Republican support.

industries.note: They would face mandatory pay-data reporting by sex, race, and ethnicity, unlimited compensatory and punitive damages, and easier class-action pay claims. Businesses argue this shifts legal risk onto them; workers who are underpaid would gain a real remedy.

The Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs would resume broad compensation-data surveys and use its full range of investigative tools on contractors, reviving enforcement programs the bill's text says were curtailed.

industries.industry: Staffing, HR compliance, and payroll data firms
industries.note: Mandatory EEOC compensation-data collection and new compliance requirements create work for firms that help employers prepare reports and defend against pay claims.
Small enterprises are exempt to the same extent as under the Fair Labor Standards Act, and would receive free federal technical-assistance materials for compliance.
